World No 2 wins back-to-back Masters to join Jack Nicklaus, Nick Faldo and Tiger Woods; check his career stats and net worthBy , Global DeskLast Updated: Apr 13, 2026, 07:16:00 AM ISTRory McIlroy achieved a historic Masters victory, successfully defending his title to join an elite group of repeat champions. He secured the win with crucial birdies around Amen Corner, overcoming late challenges to finish one shot ahead of Scottie Scheffler. This triumph marks another significant milestone in McIlroy's illustrious career.Listen to this article in summarized format Subscribe to Unlock AI Briefing and Premium ContentNew Year Offer 24 Hours LeftSubscribe NowAlready a member? Sign InWhat's IncludedAPRory McIlroy goes back-to-back at the MastersRory McIlroy added another milestone to his career at the Masters on Sunday, breaking clear of the field with two key birdies around Amen Corner. He, as is often the case, left a touch of late tension before sealing the win, etching his name into Augusta National history as only the fourth golfer to defend the title successfully in consecutive years.With another green jacket, McIlroy joined Tiger Woods, Nick Faldo, and Jack Nicklaus as the only repeat winners of the Masters. In a final round where three players had a two-shot lead, McIlroy took control with a bold shot over Rae’s Creek to 7 feet for birdie on the par-3 12th. Then he blistered a 350-yard drive on the par-5 13th that set up another birdie to move three shots ahead.There were a few tense moments along the way including a shot over the par-3 16th green that required him to use the slope to get in close for par, having to get up-and-down for par on the 17th, and a wild drive on the 18th that wound up closer to the 10th fairway. He tapped in for bogey and a 1-under 71 for a one-shot victory over Scottie Scheffler. A year ago, his playoff victory over Justin Rose made McIlroy only the sixth player with the career Grand Slam. McIlroy stood tall when he tapped in the final putt to finish at 12-under 276. It was more heartache for Rose and frustration for the others who had a chance. Rose had a two-shot lead that evaporated around Amen Corner with two bogeys and a three-putt par. He couldn't make up enough ground the rest of the way and had to settle for a third close call at the Masters.Cameron Young lost his two-shot lead much earlier with a long three-putt bogey on the par-3 sixth and taking a bogey on the next hole when he hit a wedge from the fairway into a bunker. One shot behind going to the back nine, Young closed with nine straight pars.Live EventsScottie Scheffler, the world No. 1, was in a position to potentially challenge the Masters record for the biggest 36-hole comeback in history. He started the weekend 12 shots back and had cut the deficit to just two strokes as he headed to the turn in the final round.Who is Rory McIlroy? Career and Net WorthRory McIlroy, the 36-year-old from Holywood, Northern Ireland, turned professional in 2007 and joined the PGA TOUR in 2010. He has amassed 29 PGA TOUR victories from 277 starts, with 245 cuts made and career earnings exceeding $110.1 million. Ranked No. 2 in the world (OWGR), McIlroy has collected multiple signature wins, including three in 2025 and a victory at the 2025 Masters Tournament at Augusta National Golf Club, according to the PGA Tour website.ALSO READ: Who is Rory McIlroy married to? Inside how he met wife Erica 14 years ago, filed for divorce, then reconciled within weeksMcIlroy has recorded 29 victories on the PGA TOUR, alongside 13 runner-up finishes and 11 third-place results. He has accumulated 85 top-five finishes and 134 top-10s, reflecting consistent contention at the highest level. Across his career, he has also finished inside the top 25 on 191 occasions, with two withdrawals and no disqualifications recorded. According to Celebrity Net Worth, McIlroy’s net worth is $250 million. With the latest win under his belt, McIlroy secured a Masters-record $4.5 million winner's check. That payout pushed his official PGA TOUR career earnings to a staggering $114,696,641.Energy security: The backbone of India’s AI futureEnergy security: The backbone of India’s AI futureET SpotlightLast Updated: Mar 30, 2026, 08:27:00 PM ISTThe official pre-summit ahead of the India AI Impact Summit, hosted by Hitachi Energy India, made the case that power infrastructure will determine India’s Data Center and AI leadership.Listen to this article in summarized format Subscribe to Unlock AI Briefing and Premium ContentNew Year Offer 24 Hours LeftSubscribe NowAlready a member? Sign InWhat's IncludedET SpotlightOn February 9, a different kind of AI conversation unfolded at the Taj Mahal, New Delhi. The focus was not on models, chips, or cloud architecture, but on electricity.'AI and Electric Energy: Complementing for a Sustainable and Resilient Future', the official pre-summit in the run up to the India AI Impact Summit, was hosted by Hitachi Energy India and supported by the Ministry of Electronics & IT (MeitY). It gathered policymakers, diplomats, grid operators, and academics to confront a reality the AI boom has largely sidestepped: that every data centre is a factory, every query has a power footprint, and India's ambitions to become a global AI hub can be realised if the grid keeps pace. What will really power India’s AI boom?The AI conversation starts with electricity.In his keynote at ‘AI and Electric Energy: Complementing for a Sustainable and Resilient Future’ the official pre-summit to the India AI Impact Summit hosted by Hitachi Energy India (HEI) and supported by MeitY, HEI chief executive N Venu explored how energy will shape the next phase of AI in India.In this address, he explains: • How AI and energy intertwined • Why data centres must be treated like industrial assets • How grid reliability will define technological sovereignty • Why execution speed will determine leadershipWatch the full keynote to understand why India’s AI future will be decided as much in transmission corridors as it will be in code repositories.The framing was sharp from the outset. N Venu, MD and CEO, India and South Asia, Hitachi Energy, and MD of Hitachi India, put it plainly in his opening address: "Energy is both the ultimate enabler and the ultimate bottleneck." With global data centres projected to consume close to 1,000 TWh by 2030, AI is set to become one of the important new drivers of electricity demand within five years. For India, which is already navigating a massive renewable transition, this means rethinking how power systems are expanded and operated with grid stability.The pre-summit didn't waste time on whether India was ready. It assumed readiness was a given and moved straight to execution. MeitY Secretary S Krishnan laid out the sequencing: "You start with power, then build compute, then models, and finally data. Without the foundational layer of reliable power, it is impossible to move to the next stage." His message to data centre developers was equally direct. "Data centres should not expect subsidised electricity. They must pay the full cost of power,” he underlined. India's pitch would rest on competitive tariffs, grid reliability, and speed of delivery, not handouts.That competitive advantage is real. RK Tyagi, Chairman and CMD, Power Grid Corporation of India, stated that "AI and data centres run on electrons. And in India, electrons are among the most affordable in the world." The country's visible data centre demand has doubled from around 8 GW to 16 GW, and the renewable target of 500 GW by 2030 signals serious infrastructure intent. He also emphasised that India has one of the most reliable transmission networks globally, making a case for the country as a data centre hub. The question is whether that capacity can beplanned, timed, and delivered to meet the specific demands AI workloads bring.Live EventsAnd those demands are unusual. Ghanshyam Prasad, Chairperson of the Central Electricity Authority, dismantled the misconception that data centres do not behave like constant, predictable loads. He noted that "the AI use cases we see today are barely 1-2% of what will eventually emerge," pointing to the scale of transformation ahead. They require N+1 and N+2 redundancy, meaning utilities must plan for 1.4 to 1.5 times the stated capacity to guarantee uptime. They are globally-driven, volatile, and unforgiving of even brief interruptions.“Green data centres in India cannot rely on gas. Our pathway has to be predominantly renewable,” Prasad underlined. Traditional grid planning methods, built for industrial or residential demand curves, need to be redesigned for this.The plenary session also featured international perspective on this challenge. Jan Thesleff, Ambassador of Sweden to India, stated: “Nearly 95% of Sweden's energy comes from non-fossil sources: hydro, nuclear, and wind. Our data centres are powered accordingly. This is the result of marrying digital ambition with energy responsibility." He also added that in a fragmented global environment, partnerships on grids, decarbonisation, and open standards can be constants in uncertain times. Thesleff’s message was that technological leadership without energy sovereignty is incomplete.The panel discussion that followed pushed beyond megawatt counts to the unglamorous but essential details. Abhijit Abhyankar, Professor with the Department of Electrical Engineering at IIT Delhi, noted that about 40% of all data centre power is used for cooling. He also flagged water use, a constraint India cannot afford to ignore."Fifty AI prompts can consume about half a litre of fresh water… a 100 MW data centre may consume about two million litres of fresh water daily,” he said. Reliability choices carry carbon consequences too. Batteries help, but diesel backups remain the default, bringing emissions and logistics challenges. Abhyankar’s point was not to discourage development, but to plan honestly for what operations actually require.There was also a recognition that not all the burden has to sit on the grid. Abhishek Jain, Fellow and Director of Green Economy and Impact Innovations, Council on Energy, Environment and Water (CEEW), asserted that "moving away from generalised models toward fit-for-purpose use cases is a big unlock." Moving to fit-for-purpose, agentic systems can cut inference energy significantly. He also pointed out a key inefficiency: by the time AI models 'understand' what you want, they've consumed multiple queries worth of power. Shifting certain workloads from GPU-heavy stacks to CPU-based architectures and rapid chip design improvements can also reduce the energy cost per query. India's energy strategy, he suggested, should not assume a fixed power-per-prompt ratio. That number can move, and should.Vibha Dhawan, Director General, The Energy and Resources Institute (TERI), brought the focus to adaptability. She suggested decentralised possibilities such as building-integrated solar and village-level production, while stressing that efficiency gains can dramatically change the equation, just as solar efficiency improvements already have."You don't end up reinventing the broken wheel. You complete the wheel and start using it,” she pointed out. For data centres, this means making sustainability measurable through region-specific benchmarks, water recycling, and building design, not just headline capacity.BSES Rajdhani Power Limited (BRPL) CEO Abhishek Ranjan grounded the conversation in a basic prerequisite: data. "If you don't have metering across the power systems, you won't have the data needed for correct analysis,” he said. In essence, AI can optimise grids only if grids are instrumented. Metering, sensors, and hardware upgrades are the foundation for forecasting, dispatch, and reliability. Without visibility across the power systems, ‘AI for grid’ is a slogan rather than a tool. "Move from project-to-project approaches to programme-based approaches... do it once and replicate it 10 times,” he summed up.The pre-summit closed on a definition of energy security that went beyond generation and transmission. It included skills, training, test beds, and industry-academia bridges that carry ideas from early-stage research to real deployment. N Venu summed up the stakes clearly: "The choices we make and the collaborations we forge in rooms like this will determine whether India merely participates in the AI era or leads it."India can host AI at scale, but only if it treats AI load as a serious planning input, builds measurement and flexibility into the grid, and designs sustainability around real constraints like water and materials, not just capacity headlines. The pre-summit made the case that power infrastructure is not a footnote to India's AI story. It is the opening chapter.( Originally published on Mar 02, 2026 ) (This article is generated and published by ET Spotlight team.
